Releases#

The first release goes out when every item on the release checklist is done; it is not published yet.

1bit engine is pinned upstream: every backend it builds is a submodule at a fixed commit (third_party/), and the bump-* workflows open a PR whenever an upstream moves. The engine runs inside Lemonade, which releases on Fridays. The release run (scripts/weekly.sh) rebuilds everything from scratch at the current pins, so each release carries that week's upstreams.

Releases are tagged v<ISO year>.<ISO week> (v2026.40), like Lemonade's 2026.39.1; a second release in the same week gets .1.

What moved since the last rehearsal (18 Oct)#

Every line is a merged PR; the numbers are measured, and the ones measured on Strix Halo carry the power state they were taken in. lemonade bench standard = Lemonade's own CI benchmark (reload before every run); ours = our sampler/batched standard (see the table legend in the auto-opt database).

HRX speed (ours). Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_XL with MTP, greedy 256-token chats: 36.0 / 26.8 / 29.9 tok/s on code / prose / short, from 25.9 / 20.5 / 21.9 before the speculative verify pass was reworked — the step it took is 121 ms to 88 ms per step (#487). Decode without MTP stays 12.2 tok/s.

Batched, ours standard (N concurrent 256-token chat requests, -c 8192 per slot, median of 3, 90 W cap, PCM pad (23 Oct)), aggregate tok/s at N=8: Qwen3.8-27B 50.7 (2.08x N=1, with the model's own MTP draft), Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B 138.1 (1.64x), Qwen3.5-4B 194.3 (3.39x). Single stream in the same cells: Coder-30B 84.2, 27B 24.3 (MTP on; 12.2 without), Qwen3.5-4B 57.3. Lemonade's Vulkan build reaches 245.7 on Coder-30B at N=8 in the same run — that gap is batching headroom, not a model result, and it is the next speed row.

Correctness and placement. Strict device placement is the default: a graph with any node off HRX refuses to load, and the hardware gate fails the same condition (#482, #473, #442). The census closes 43 of 43 configurations with 0 nodes off the GPU and one graph split (#476, #480, #481), the gate now covers q8_0 KV rows, a mixed K/V flash-attention case, an MoE model, an IQ quant and a second needle (#474, #477, #484), and the KLD bases were re-recorded at the release pin (#456). #315 is resolved: the CWSR-on soak passed 37 arms over 9 h 03 min with 0 faults (#518), after the CWSR save area moved into GTT (#454) and hrx-system gained its HRX_ALLOW_NO_SVM gate (#455). A lost GPU now exits the server instead of serving from a broken context (#466), allocation safety bounds the program cache and poisons a device after a fault (#486), and the ZAYA1-8B NaN re-check closed on 120 fresh loads, 0 NaN at the current pins (#433).

NPU (sealed). The gate gained an NPU phase and the packages carry only the sealed kernel sets — a plaintext artifact fails the packaging check, and the launcher refuses an unsealed one (#503, #505, #509, #512). The 0.6B gate phase measures 90.33 tok/s; the OS image proves amd_pmf sensors and the NPU from the booted image (#517, #523). The runtime's public header and prebuilt-library build are in the tree (#467, #479, #469).

Lemonade. One hop for GGUFs: Lemonade starts the engine's llama-server directly, no shim (#475, fork #15), the engine's own warm-ups are sent in order (#492, fork #16, #17), and the Ubuntu 26.04 PPA's lemond runs our HRX server unchanged (#483). Synced to upstream #3771 (fork #21, #520). The catalog has 22 HRX entries, each proven on the box — strict placement, one request in role, lemonade bench ... chat-short — and 3 NPU entries (fork #19, #20, #23); chat-short spans 43.4 (Qwen3-8B) to 330.7 tok/s (Qwen3-0.6B), 0 faults in 16 holds.

1bit OS. The image carries the sealed NPU sets and the new Lemonade (#512, #523), the UKI is signed with the enrolled MOK so a stick boots with Secure Boot on (#513), the USB4 v2 / Thunderbolt stack is loaded (#514), and amd_pmf sensors come up from the booted image (#517). The install step is not in this candidate (branch 1bit/os-install).

Tooling. scripts/gpu-hold: a fair FIFO GPU queue, used by the hardware gate and the release runs, which honours the box's thermal brake and cools down after a hot hold (#501, #502). Census and pins kept current daily (#506, #524), and the kernel is now a written runbook with a rehearsal at v7.3 and linux-next next-20261022 (#525).

What a release carries#

file what
lemonade-onebit-<tag>-linux-x86_64.tar.zst Lemonade (lemond, lemonade, its web app) from our fork with the onebit recipe, and the engine in 1bit/: 1bit and every backend: HRX (and the CPU, from the same llama-server), DwarfStar, and the NPU engine's runtime (the NPU route is in progress, below). No Vulkan or ROCm llama.cpp since RFC #213 stage 3
1bit-os-<tag>.img.zst, 1bit-os-<tag>.efi 1bit OS, a Lemonade appliance with the engine as a bootable USB image (os/README.md)
changes.json, SHA256SUMS what moved upstream since the last release, as data; checksums

The engine is embedded in Lemonade, so it ships only inside those two: there is no standalone engine tarball and no Windows package (Lemonade has its own Windows build). On the GPU the engine is pure HRX with HIP kernels: no Vulkan, ROCm backend, Metal, ZINC or CUDA. Lemonade serves those with its own backends.

The engine in 1bit/ keeps the build tree's layout (scripts/package-linux.sh): 1bit finds each backend at the same path relative to itself as in the build (app/built_path.h), and every program finds its libraries beside itself. Unpack the package anywhere and start Lemonade through lemond-onebit, which points Lemonade's onebit backend at the packaged 1bit (LEMONADE_ONEBIT_BIN):

tar --zstd -xf lemonade-onebit-v2026.40-linux-x86_64.tar.zst
lemonade-onebit-v2026.40/lemond-onebit           # lemond with the onebit recipe on the packaged engine

The builds target Strix Halo: the llama.cpp backends are built with GGML_NATIVE on its Zen 5. HRX needs TheRock in /opt/rocm-therock; the NPU needs the amdxdna kernel driver. The closed NPU add-ons (NPU engine) are never in a release.

The NPU engine#

The release is the HRX runtime with our HIP kernels and the NPU engine, all inside Lemonade. The release carries the NPU runtime, compiled into 1bit, and the onebit recipe's npu backend. The NPU kernels are closed too: they ship as sealed artifacts that 1bit verifies and opens in memory at load, failing cleanly on a wrong key with no network callback of any kind; a lifted kernel file is ciphertext and does not run (NPU engine). The release package carries them, and serves dense Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) on the NPU.

scripts/weekly.sh packs them by default (WEEKLY_NPU_KERNELS=0 builds without): the sealed kernel sets go beside 1bit in npu/kernels, the build loads sealed kernels only (ONEBIT_NPU_RELEASE), the lemond-onebit launcher sets ONEBIT_KCRYPT_REQUIRE_SEALED=1, and the package checks refuse a plaintext kernel, an ELF for anything but the host, a symbol table in 1bit, or a private source name in it. The release machine holds the kernel key in ONEBIT_NPU_KEY_DIR (default ~/.config/1bit-npu-key).

Sealing is confidentiality; each set is signed too (#574). Before a set is packed it gets manifest.json - every file the set ships, with the sha256 of its ciphertext - and manifest.sig, Ed25519 over that manifest by the release signing key (tools/seal_manifest.py write <set> --key <release key>, ONEBIT_SEAL_KEY). Packaging requires both: scripts/package-linux.sh and the weekly package_checks refuse a set without them or a manifest that does not match the files packed, and verify the signatures when ONEBIT_SEAL_PUB names the release public key. 1bit-release-check proves the same on a written stick, so a set that was re-sealed or swapped fails the checks even though it still opens.

Private components#

Two components of the release binaries are proprietary and compiled in; their source is not in this repository or in any release. They ship under the 1bit Binary License: anyone may use them for any purpose, including commercial use, and pass on exact unmodified copies with the license and notices; modifying them, reverse engineering them (except where the law expressly allows it) and removing notices are not allowed. The third-party code inside them is listed with its licenses in NOTICE-BINARY. Every release package and the 1bit OS image carry both files beside the engine's LICENSE and NOTICE:

Component Compiled into Pin Build option
The 1bit NPU runtime (NPU engine) 1bit (static) config/npu-runtime.config ONEBIT_NPU_RT_DIR (or a prebuilt ONEBIT_NPU_RT_LIB)
The private HIP kernels for HRX (HRX, "Private HIP kernels") hrx/llama/bin/libggml-hrx.so (code objects) config/gpu-kernels.config ONEBIT_GPU_PRIVATE

The build stage fetches each with scripts/fetch-private.sh <pin> <dir>: the pinned path at the pinned commit only, with the release machine's gh login (read access to the private repositories). The run stops if either cannot be fetched or is not at its pinned sha. Move a pin by hand, after the NPU check or the HRX checks on Strix Halo.

The public binary drop#

A source build outside the org has no private HIP kernels and no private NPU runtime, so it cannot compile those parts itself. scripts/make-binary-drop.sh <engine checkout> <out dir> packs them already compiled, for one engine pin, as binary-drop-<version>.tar.zst + SHA256SUMS:

binary-drop-<version>/
  hrx/llama/bin/        llama-server, llama-bench and the libraries beside them, libggml-hrx.so
                        with the private HIP kernels compiled in
  npu/libnpu_rt_api.a   the NPU runtime behind the engine's public npu/npu_rt_api.h
  npu/include/          npu_rt_api.h (the engine's own public header)
  LICENSE-BINARY NOTICE-BINARY LICENSE NOTICE
  MANIFEST              the pins below, the build host, the compilers, sha256 of every file

It takes the HRX tree from a release build (--build <dir>, packed the way package-linux.sh packs it: the same scripts/pack-elf.sh steps copy the libraries it loads beside it, set RUNPATH to $ORIGIN and strip it) or from an already packed release (--from-package <tar.zst>), and the NPU library either prebuilt (--npu-lib) or built from the pinned private sources (--npu-rt <dir>, its build-api-lib.sh). It then runs the same class of checks the release package runs: the NPU runtime compiled in, the kernels really are compiled in, no source files, nothing named like the private sources, both binary licenses present, every library found. It publishes nothing; the orchestrator publishes the tarball and adds its line to config/binary-drop.config.

To build against a drop, point CMake at it — a directory or the tarball's URL:

cmake -B build -DONEBIT_HRX=ON -DONEBIT_NPU=ON -DONEBIT_BINARY_DROP=/path/to/binary-drop-<version>
# or -DONEBIT_BINARY_DROP=https://…/binary-drop-<version>.tar.zst

A URL is only accepted when config/binary-drop.config pins its sha256 for the engine commit being built (drop=<engine sha> <version> <sha256>); file(DOWNLOAD) refuses a body that does not match. A directory is verified against its MANIFEST — every file's sha256, and the engine commit it was built from — and a mismatch, or a drop built for another commit, stops the configure. With a drop in place, ONEBIT_GPU_PRIVATE and ONEBIT_NPU_RT_DIR are not needed and not used: the build links hrx/llama/bin/llama-server and npu/libnpu_rt_api.a from the drop, and does not build llama.cpp, so the llama.cpp and hrx-system submodules are not required either. HRX still needs TheRock's HSA runtime on the machine that runs it.

The NPU engine's runtime is compiled into 1bit; no packed program needs a separate NPU runtime library. scripts/package-linux.sh strips every packed program and library (strip --strip-unneeded) and makes each find its libraries beside itself ($ORIGIN, scripts/pack-elf.sh), with LLVM's OpenMP runtime (libomp.so, which the HRX llama.cpp libraries link when TheRock's amdclang builds them; credited in NOTICE-BINARY) packed in hrx/llama/bin. After packing the engine tarball the package stage checks (logs/package-checks.log; a failure stops the release):

  • Self-contained NPU runtime: for the build's 1bit and every program and library in the tarball, no separate NPU runtime library is needed or packed.
  • Kernels in: the packed libggml-hrx.so exports the add-on's ggml_hrx_hip_addon_register.
  • No source: no source file (.hip, .c, .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .h, .hpp, .inc, .cu, .cmake) and no file named like one of the private checkouts' files. The three public GGUF-on-NPU helper scripts are the stated exception: scripts/repack_gguf.py, its declared-scale guard scripts/check_repack_config.py and the lane packer tools/gguf_to_q4nx.py are the engine's own Apache-2.0 source, published in this repository, and a packed install cannot serve a GGUF on the NPU without them (NPU engine). The check fails if a tarball carrying the NPU kernels is missing any of the three.
  • Licensed: LICENSE, NOTICE, LICENSE-BINARY and NOTICE-BINARY are in the tarball.
  • Libraries found: ldd (with ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1) finds every library each packed program and library needs, except the TheRock runtime the package documents (HIP, hipBLAS(Lt), rocBLAS, HSA, which DwarfStar links).
  • Links inside: every symlink in the engine tarball and in the Lemonade + onebit tarball is relative and resolves inside the package (pack_outside_links); the libggml*.so -> .so.0 links stay links. Lemonade's build links its web app's KaTeX fonts to the build machine's /usr/share/fonts/truetype/katex; the package stage and os/mini/mkimage.sh copy every link that points out of the tree as a file (pack_localize_links, scripts/pack-elf.sh).
  • Web app: the Lemonade + onebit tarball carries Lemonade's web app (bin/resources/web-app/index.html), the UI lemond serves at /, as 1bit OS does.

SHA256SUMS is written again by the release stage, after changes.json, so it covers every file.

To exercise only the private builds and the packaging without releasing, on Strix Halo:

WEEKLY_DRY_RUN=1 WEEKLY_TAG=rehearsal-private scripts/weekly.sh ~/.cache/1bit-weekly build package

The release run#

scripts/weekly.sh <workdir> on Strix Halo, in stages:

  1. bumps: each open bump-* PR is merged onto main locally, built with every backend, and tested: ctest (with the serve end-to-end tests on Qwen3-0.6B) plus the check that bump needs, below. A PR that passes is brought up to date, waits for CI, and is merged. One that fails stays open, and the release lists it as held back.
  2. build and test: main at the merged pins, the same way.
  3. package: the two packages above. scripts/package-linux.sh packs the engine first; its tarball goes into the Lemonade + onebit package as 1bit/, not into the release on its own.
  4. release: tools/weekly_changes.py lists, for every pin that moved since the last release, the upstream commits (authors, PRs) and releases in between; that becomes the release notes and changes.json, and gh release create publishes it all.

WEEKLY_DRY_RUN=1 merges and publishes nothing; stages can be run one at a time (scripts/weekly.sh ~/.cache/1bit-weekly build test).

Before the first stage runs, weekly.sh checks what the machine must have (the 2026-10-19 rehearsal found these only after the build) and stops with a message naming what is missing:

  • bumps, build: TheRock in /opt/rocm-therock, or -DONEBIT_HRX_TOOLCHAIN=<dir> in WEEKLY_CMAKE_ARGS; hipcc for DwarfStar, in TheRock or /opt/rocm, or ROCM_PATH.
  • package: patchelf (scripts/package-linux.sh); node and npm for Lemonade's web app (LEMONADE_WEB_APP=1 scripts/build-lemonade.sh; its npm ci needs the network); a readable kernel image for 1bit OS, /boot/vmlinuz-$(uname -r) or VMLINUZ=<copy> (Ubuntu's /boot/vmlinuz-* is root-only). Which kernel that image should carry, and how a new one is built, signed and gated before it is allowed on the box, is Linux kernel. The image's licences step copies from the submodules of the run's own checkout (<workdir>/src, checked out by the build stage), so run os/mini/mkimage.sh from there, not from a plain worktree without submodules.

Bumps#

PR check beyond build + ctest
bump-lemonade/* Lemonade's LLM suite through the onebit recipe on HRX (Lemonade)
bump-laya/* tests/laya_route_e2e.sh on the pinned checkpoint
bump-ds4/* DwarfStar's routed-MoE test (DS4_TEST=1 scripts/build-ds4.sh)
bump-hrx/* every hrx row of registry/check_models.tsv through tools/registry_check.py (serve end to end per architecture, ZAYA1 and the Qwen MoE models included); any FAIL holds the bump
bump-xdna/*, bump-tokenizers/* covered by build + ctest (serve end to end on each device); the xdna-driver pin is the amdxdna kernel driver, which the release does not build: check it on Strix Halo with the module loaded (NPU engine, "The XDNA driver")

A pin bump raised by hand (rather than by one of those workflows) has to do what the workflow does, or the gates above silently do not apply to it (engine#672):

  • branch it bump-<name>/<sha> or add the hw-gate label - hw-gate.yml runs on bump-hrx/* or on that label (it reads hw_gate: skipping otherwise, which looks like a pass), and scripts/weekly.sh's bumps stage only picks up bump-* heads, so a differently named branch is invisible to the Sunday run as well;
  • carry the data derived from the pinned backends: registry/architectures.json is generated (tools/registry_build.py with the submodules at their pins), and a class that starts being mapped needs its reviewed entry in registry/significant.json (mapped_ok, or --check-gaps refuses it) plus its expectation in tests/census_watch_test.py updated - otherwise registry_pins and census_watch fail at the new pin (engine#672: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash went from "reviewed report-only" to mapped);
  • run the checks in the table above, plus hw-gate (see Hardware gate, "When it runs").

Before the build, every bump also checks that each pin it moves is on the branch .gitmodules names for that submodule (GitHub's compare API: the branch equals or contains the pin). A pin off its branch is held: the shallow clones follow the branch and cannot fetch it, and GitHub may drop an unreferenced commit.

The announcement#

After the release, the 1bit engine Discord gets a new post in #announcements, written from changes.json in the layout of Lemonade's release posts: what the week brings, the notable upstream changes with credit to their authors, the rest as a list, and the downloads (the two packages above). Then two lists written straight from the data: New models (repos published under our Hugging Face org, models added to Lemonade's catalog, architectures the registry gained or that gained a backend) and Updates (every upstream as pinned in the release, with its latest release and changelog). Each release gets its own post, and earlier ones stay.
